turns.question: Where do we have to sue Brennan under the services agreement, and do we get a jury?
turns.text:
The Warehousing and Distribution Services Agreement between Hollis and Brennan specifies that any action arising from the agreement must be brought in the Superior Court of the State of Delaware, Complex Commercial Litigation Division (CCLD). This is stated in the agreement [10] Additionally, the agreement states that each party irrevocably consents to the personal jurisdiction of that court and waives any objection to venue there.

Regarding the jury trial, the agreement explicitly states that each party knowingly, voluntarily, and irrevocably waives any right to a trial by jury in any action or proceeding arising out of or relating to the agreement. This is quoted as: [10]

Therefore, under the terms of the agreement, any legal action against Brennan must be filed in the Superior Court of the State of Delaware, Complex Commercial Litigation Division, and there will be no jury trial.

turns.question: What's Brennan's liability cap now, after the First Amendment?
turns.text:
The First Amendment to the Warehousing and Distribution Services Agreement (January 15, 2026) states that "Brennan's aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed One Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollars ($1,500,000) in any Contract Year" [1].

The First Amendment also clarifies that Section 12.2, as amended, applies to all claims arising on or after the Amendment Effective Date [1].

Furthermore, the First Amendment specifies that Sections 12.1 and 12.3 of the Agreement are not amended and continue in full force and effect [1].

turns.question: Brennan's paperwork says HMS-26-0588 was delivered June 3. When did it actually show up?

turns.question: Ostrow Kaplan says Brennan's exposure is capped at $500K under Section 12.2. Is that right?
turns.text:
The documents in this matter indicate that Ostrow Kaplan's statement about Brennan's exposure being capped at $500K under Section 12.2 is not accurate. According to the Complaint, Section 12.2 of the Agreement, as amended by the First Amendment, limits Brennan's aggregate liability to $1,500,000 in any Contract Year [7].

However, the original Section 12.2 in the Warehousing and Distribution Services Agreement states that Brennan's aggregate liability shall not exceed $500,000 in any Contract Year [1].

Additionally, the Demand letter to Brennan Freight Lines mentions that the First Amendment replaced Section 12.2, and the cap on Brennan's aggregate liability is now $1,500,000 in any Contract Year [6].

turns.question: What late delivery credit do we have coming on HMS-26-0588?
turns.text:
The documents indicate that Brennan Freight Lines issued a credit memo, BFL-CM-26-019, for $1,150.00, which reverses only the freight charge for Shipment HMS-26-0588 [5]. This credit was issued as a customer accommodation and is not an admission of liability [5].

According to the Newark DC receiving log, Shipment HMS-26-0588 was received on June 6, 2026, at 9:40 a.m. [6]. However, Brennan denies that it is liable for any late delivery credit, stating that the shipment was delivered less than one full day after the end of the Delivery Window [2].

The documents do not provide any further details about a late delivery credit beyond the $1,150.00 credit memo.

turns.question: Brennan's counsel says our June 9 notice was late because 9.3 only gives us 48 hours. Were we on time?
turns.text:
The June 9 notice was sent by Patricia Lowell on June 9, 2026, and was acknowledged by Gregory Halvorsen on June 11, 2026 [1]. Brennan's counsel claims that 9.3 only gives 48 hours for notice, stating that "Section 9.3 of the Agreement requires the customer to give notice of any claim 'within forty-eight (48) hours of delivery'" [4]. The Shipment was delivered on June 3, 2026, and the notice was sent on June 9, which is six days later [4].

The documents do not state whether the June 9 notice was timely under Section 9.3. turns.question: What did FDA find in the cracker samples, and what does the warning letter charge Meadowgate with?
turns.text:
The FDA found that the cracker samples contained sesame, a major food allergen, which was not declared on the label. Specifically, the FDA laboratory analysis found 14 ppm of sesame in the sample from lot HG2608B and 38 ppm in the sample from lot HG2609A [1].

The warning letter charges Meadowgate with misbranding under section 403(w) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The charge is that the finished product contains sesame, a major food allergen, but the label does not declare it. The product label declares "Contains: Wheat, Soy," but sesame is not included in the ingredient list or in the "Contains" statement [1][2].
